column4: The section explicitly names the concealment sense of its و ر ي root; this ayah uses “وُورِيَ” for what was covered from Adam and his wife. It adds bodily concealment to the section’s burial-and-uncovering image.
After the hidden shame is exposed, this ayah says the pair begin covering themselves with leaves. It completes 7:20’s concealment detail with a specific exposure-then-covering action.

This parallel account says the pair’s nakedness became visible and they began patching leaves over themselves. It repeats the concealment-and-exposure action in a second Qur’anic telling, related to the section’s hidden things brought into view.

The verse uses the section’s named ث و ر root in “فَتُثِيرُ سَحَابًا”: winds stir clouds up. It confirms the root’s stirring or raising action in a different medium, extending the image from hooves and soil to wind and cloud.

This ayah says God revives the earth after its death and explicitly likens that to raising the dead. It supplies a direct life-from-earth parallel to the section’s graves opened and hidden contents raised.
“تَشَقَّقُ الْأَرْضُ عَنْهُمْ سِرَاعًا” depicts the earth splitting away from people as they hurry out, a direct scene of buried people emerging from the ground.
This ayah says people come swiftly out of graves on the Day, directly staging the grave opening described in the section and adding their hurried movement toward the gathering.

Immediately after the grave emergence in 70:43, this ayah says their eyes are humbled and disgrace covers them. It adds the exposed people’s condition, a reversal of earthly confidence before the final disclosure.

In the food-and-crops passage, this ayah says God splits the earth open; the following verses show grain and other growth emerging. It gives a literal soil-opening scene parallel to the section’s turned ground, though for cultivation rather than graves.

“وَإِذَا الْأَرْضُ مُدَّتْ” describes earth spread out immediately before 84:4 says it casts out what is within and empties. This ayah supplies the opened, flattened ground that frames the section’s contents emerging.
After earth ejects its burdens in 99:2, people ask what has happened to it. That bewildered response complements the section’s “does he not know?” question about grave contents being brought out.

After 99:4 says earth reports its news, this ayah attributes that disclosure to the Lord’s inspiration. It adds the divine source behind the earth’s testimony, alongside the section’s final notice that the Lord is fully informed.

This ayah says people come forth in separate groups to be shown their deeds. It carries 99:1–4’s earth upheaval into the exposure of human actions, parallel to the section’s sequence from opened graves to extracted breast contents.

Here earth and mountains are carried and crushed in one crushing blow, in the same judgment passage that later presents people with nothing hidden. The terrain’s violent overturning intensifies the section’s image of earth opened at the end.

The section’s dictionary entry for ح ص ل describes precious metal extracted from ore; this ayah shows metal heated for ornaments or use, with the waste disappearing while what benefits people remains. It gives the extraction and separation image an explicit Qur’anic scene and a criterion of what endures.

The section’s mineral sense names gold and silver recovered from earth; this ayah names people who hoard gold and silver. It turns the extracted treasure into stored wealth whose moral value is exposed by the surrounding judgment warning.

The next ayah says the hoarded metals are heated in Hellfire and used to brand their owners. It joins the section’s metal and fire images in a reversal where treasure becomes evidence against its possessor.

This ayah speaks of good things brought forth from earth and forbids choosing the bad for charity when one would not accept it except reluctantly. It parallels the section’s ore-sifting image through a concrete distinction between valued and inferior produce from earth.

This ayah says people extract ornaments from the sea. The section’s dictionary account of metal recovery from mineral soil gives a specific parallel of valuable material drawn from a natural store, with the source here being water rather than earth.

The ayah contrasts fresh and salt waters, then says people extract wearable ornaments from them. It repeats the extraction image with a distinct focus on the two sources and the valuables each yields.

The section’s dictionary form describes precious material extracted from stone; this ayah pictures water bursting from split stone. The substance differs, but both make a hidden content emerge from rock.

This ayah pictures vegetation from rain drying into chaff that winds scatter. It parallels the section’s named بعثر dictionary sense of dispersing and scattering things, in an earthly scene of what appears and then passes away.

After a ruined town prompts a question about life after death, God restores the traveler’s donkey’s bones and covers them with flesh. This concrete restoration of what has decayed in the earth parallels the section’s dead brought out from graves.

This ayah moves from human formation out of dust to dead earth stirred and raised into growth. It joins the section’s earth-turning image to the broader cycle of life emerging from apparently lifeless ground.

Qarun’s treasures have keys heavy enough to burden a group of strong men. This gives a concrete treasure-and-load counterpart to the section’s picture of grave contents as hidden cargo and its extraction of valuable material from earth.
The earth swallows Qarun and his house. This reverses the section’s direction: there, earth is turned so hidden contents come out; here, a wealthy man and his home disappear into it.

After the swallowing in 28:81, people who had wished for Qarun’s position realize that God could have made the earth swallow them too. It completes the wealth-to-earth reversal with the bystanders’ changed judgment of worldly riches.

The section’s ث و ر dictionary entry says locusts take flight; this ayah names locusts among the plagues sent against Pharaoh. The link is limited to the same specific swarm creature: here it is a destructive worldly plague, unlike the resurrection simile in 54:7.
